paragraphs: The law is the declaration of the general will; in the same way, the censorship is the declaration of the public judgment. Public opinion is the kind of law the censor administers, and like the prince, he applies it only to particular cases.
Far from being the arbiter of the people’s opinion, the censorial tribunal only declares it, and as soon as the two part company, its decisions are null and void.

It is useless to distinguish the morals of a nation from the things it esteems; both depend on the same principle and cannot be told apart. There is no people on earth whose choice of pleasures is decided by nature rather than opinion. Set men’s opinions right, and their morals will purify themselves. Men always love what is good, or what they find good; it is in judging what is good that they go wrong. So it is this judgment that must be regulated. Whoever judges of morals judges of honor, and whoever judges of honor finds his law in opinion.

The opinions of a people come from its constitution. Although the law does not regulate morals, it is legislation that gives them birth. When legislation grows weak, morals degenerate; but in such cases the judgment of the censors will not accomplish what the force of the laws has failed to do.

It follows that the censorship may be useful for preserving morals, but can never be useful for restoring them. Set up censors while the laws are vigorous; once the laws have lost their vigor, all hope is gone, for no legitimate power can keep its force when the laws have lost theirs.

The censorship upholds morals by preventing opinion from growing corrupt, by keeping it upright through wise applications, and sometimes even by fixing it when it is still uncertain. The use of seconds in duels had been carried to wild extremes in the kingdom of France. It was done away with merely by these words in a royal edict: “As for those who are cowards enough to call upon seconds.” This judgment, by anticipating the public’s, decided it at once. But when edicts from the same source tried to declare duelling itself an act of cowardice, as indeed it is, the public took no notice. Common opinion does not regard it as cowardice, and on this point the public’s mind was already made up.

I have stated elsewhere[1] that since public opinion is not subject to any constraint, there need be no trace of constraint in the tribunal set up to represent it. It is impossible to admire too much the art with which the Romans, and still more the Lacedaemonians, used this resource, which we moderns have wholly lost.

A man of bad morals made a good proposal in the Spartan Council. The Ephors ignored it and had a virtuous citizen make the same proposal. What an honor for the one, and what a disgrace for the other, with no praise or blame given to either! Some drunkards from Samos[2] defiled the tribunal of the Ephors. The next day a public edict gave the Samians permission to be filthy. An actual punishment would not have been as severe as such impunity. Once Sparta has pronounced on what is right or wrong, Greece makes no appeal against her judgments.
